Assignment 6: Parole Reform

  • Show All Code

  • View Source

MUSA 5080 · Fall 2026

Author

Qiwen Bian

Published

November 13, 2026

The scenario

The Georgia Department of Community Supervision is considering a risk model to guide parole decisions. Every person released to parole would get a predicted probability of being rearrested within three years. The department has two proposed uses:

  • Use A: people above a threshold get more restrictive supervision (more check-ins, electronic monitoring, faster revocation).
  • Use B: people above a threshold get priority for reentry services (housing assistance, job placement, a case manager).

The department has promised that the model will not use race. You’ve been hired to build it and to tell them whether that promise means what they think it means.

What you’re turning in: this rendered document, published in the assignments/ folder of your portfolio.

How this assignment works: it has less scaffolding than earlier ones. The Week 11 lab (COMPAS) is your fully worked example: almost every step here has a matching step there. Where the NIJ data behaves differently from COMPAS, the instructions below tell you. Everywhere else, adapt the lab code yourself.

A5 part Week 11 lab step
3.1 odds ratios Step 3
4.1 predictions + confusion matrix Steps 4–5
4.3 threshold sweep Step 5 (rates_at())
4.4 ROC + AUC Step 6
5.1–5.2 errors by race Step 7
5.3 what carries race in Step 8

Two differences from the lab: the outcome is called recid (not two_year_recid), and you fit on train and evaluate on test. In the lab we fit and scored on the same data. So every predict() in Parts 4 and 5 needs newdata = test.

The data

The National Institute of Justice’s Recidivism Forecasting Challenge data: 25,835 people released from Georgia prisons to parole supervision, 2013–2015. Download the CSV from Canvas, put it in your portfolio’s data/ folder, and rename it nij_recidivism.csv.

A few things to know before you start:

  • Race is recorded only as Black or white. The data includes no one else.
  • Counts are top-coded: “10 or more” prior felony arrests is stored as text. parse_number() turns it into 10, which undercounts people with many more.
  • Residence_PUMA is not a census PUMA code. NIJ grouped Georgia’s PUMAs into 25 areas and numbered them 1–25 to protect privacy. You can use it to group people by place, but you can’t map it.
  • Training_Sample is NIJ’s own train/test split. Use it.

Part 1: Load and clean

Code 
library(tidyverse)

# rendering inside the project runs from the portfolio root; standalone runs
# from this folder, so check both
data_csv <- if (file.exists("assignment6-data/nij_recidivism.csv")) {
  "assignment6-data/nij_recidivism.csv"
} else {
  "assignments/assignment6-data/nij_recidivism.csv"
}

nij <- read_csv(data_csv) %>%
  mutate(
    recid              = as.integer(Recidivism_Within_3years),
    male               = as.integer(Gender == "M"),
    age_group          = factor(Age_at_Release),
    prison_years       = factor(Prison_Years,
                                levels = c("Less than 1 year", "1-2 years",
                                           "Greater than 2 to 3 years",
                                           "More than 3 years")),
    prior_fel_arrests  = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Felony),
    prior_misd_arrests = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Misd),
    puma               = factor(Residence_PUMA)
  )

train <- nij %>% filter(Training_Sample == 1)
test  <- nij %>% filter(Training_Sample == 0)

nij %>%
  mutate(sample = if_else(Training_Sample == 1, "train", "test")) %>%
  group_by(sample) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), rearrested = sum(recid),
            share_rearrested = mean(recid), .groups = "drop")

Your answer: All 3,167 missing values are for women. Adding Gang_Affiliated as is would exclude all 2,217 women from the training fit and leave all 950 women in the test set without predictions.

Part 2: What would you know at the moment of decision?

The parole decision happens at release. Some columns in this file were recorded during the three years of supervision that followed.

2.1 Sort every predictor column into one of two lists. You don’t need code; use names(nij) and the column names.

Known at release Recorded during supervision (leakage)
Gender, Race, Age_at_Release, Residence_PUMA, Gang_Affiliated Violations_ElectronicMonitoring, Violations_Instruction, Violations_FailToReport, Violations_MoveWithoutPermission, Delinquency_Reports
Supervision_Risk_Score_First, Supervision_Level_First, Education_Level, Dependents, Prison_Offense, Prison_Years Program_Attendances, Program_UnexcusedAbsences, Residence_Changes
All eight Prior_Arrest_Episodes_* and all eight Prior_Conviction_Episodes_* columns Avg_Days_per_DrugTest, DrugTests_THC_Positive, DrugTests_Cocaine_Positive, DrugTests_Meth_Positive, DrugTests_Other_Positive
Prior_Revocations_Parole, Prior_Revocations_Probation, Condition_MH_SA, Condition_Cog_Ed, Condition_Other Percent_Days_Employed, Jobs_Per_Year, Employment_Exempt

2.2 Pick one variable from the right-hand column and explain, in two sentences, why including it would make your model look better than it really is.

Your answer: Percent_Days_Employed is measured after release, and rearrest can cut the observation period short. Including it would give the model future information and make its test performance look better than it would be at release.

3.2 Constant on the odds, not on the probability. Use predict(..., type = "response") with newdata to compute the predicted probability for two made-up people, then add one prior felony arrest to each:

  • a man, age 23–27, 1–2 years in prison, 2 prior felony arrests, 1 misdemeanor arrest
  • a man, age 48 or older, 1–2 years in prison, 2 prior felony arrests, 1 misdemeanor arrest

How much does one more arrest change each person’s probability? Why are the two changes different?

Code 
people <- tibble(
  male               = c(1, 1),
  age_group          = factor(c("23-27", "48 or older"), levels = levels(nij$age_group)),
  prison_years       = factor(c("1-2 years", "1-2 years"), levels = levels(nij$prison_years)),
  prior_fel_arrests  = c(2, 2),
  prior_misd_arrests = c(1, 1)
)

people_plus_one <- people %>%
  mutate(prior_fel_arrests = prior_fel_arrests +1)

people %>%
  transmute(
    age_group,
    before = predict(base_fit, newdata = people, type = "response"),
    after = predict(base_fit, newdata = people_plus_one, type = "response"),
    change_pp = 100 * (after - before)
  )

Your answer: The 23–27-year-old goes from 56.45% to 60.51%, up 4.06 percentage points. The person aged 48 or older goes from 17.86% to 20.45%, up 2.59 points. The same odds multiplier produces a larger probability change near 50%.

3.3 Improve the model. Add at least three predictors from your “known at release” list. Keep race out. Call it my_fit. In two or three sentences, say what you added and why you expected each one to help.

WarningCheck for missing values before you add a variable

Some columns have blanks: Prison_Offense is missing for about 1 in 8 people, and Supervision_Level_First for about 1 in 15. If you add one as it is, glm() silently drops those people from training, and predict() returns NA for them in test. Then mean() gives NA in Parts 4–6, and table() quietly leaves them out. Either leave the variable out, or keep the blanks as their own category, for example mutate(offense = replace_na(Prison_Offense, "Missing")). Whichever you choose, say so in your answer.

Code 
add_predictors <- function(data){
  data %>%
    mutate(
      education = factor(Education_Level),
      prior_violent_arrests = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Violent),
      prior_property_arrests = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Property)
    )
}
train <- add_predictors(train)
test <- add_predictors(test)

added <- c("education", "prior_violent_arrests", "prior_property_arrests")
stopifnot(!anyNA(train[added]), !anyNA(test[added]))

my_fit <- glm(recid ~ male + age_group + prison_years + prior_fel_arrests + 
    prior_misd_arrests + education + prior_violent_arrests + prior_property_arrests,
  family = binomial, 
  data = train, 
  na.action = na.fail
)

summary(my_fit)

Part 4: Choosing a threshold

4.1 Add a column p_hat to test with predicted probabilities from my_fit, and a column pred_50 that flags anyone at or above 0.5. (Parts 5 and 6 use these column names.) Then make a confusion matrix and compute sensitivity and specificity.

Code 
test <- test %>%
  mutate(
    p_hat = predict(my_fit, newdata = test, type = "response"),
    pred_50 = as.integer(p_hat >= 0.5)
  )

table(predicted = test$pred_50, actual = test$recid)
         actual
predicted    0    1
        0 1504  805
        1 1820 3678
Code 
test %>%
  summarize(
    sensitivity = sum(pred_50 == 1 & recid == 1) / sum(recid == 1),
    specificity = sum(pred_50 == 0 & recid == 0) / sum(recid == 0),
    accuracy    = mean(pred_50 == recid)
  )
# A tibble: 1 × 3
  sensitivity specificity accuracy
        <dbl>       <dbl>    <dbl>
1       0.820       0.452    0.664

Your answer: Sensitivity was 82.0% and specificity was 45.2%.

4.2 What share of the test set does your model label “high risk” at 0.5? Compare it to the share actually rearrested. What does that tell you about 0.5 as a default for this data?

Your answer: The 0.50 cutoff flagged 70.4% of the test set, while 57.4% were rearrested. It also flagged 54.8% of people who were not rearrested, making it a poor automatic default for restrictive supervision.

4.3 Compute sensitivity and specificity for every threshold from 0.30 to 0.80 in steps of 0.05, and plot both lines on one chart with threshold on the x-axis.

Hint: in the lab you called rates_at() three times by hand. Here you need eleven thresholds. map_dfr(thresholds, function(t) ...) runs the same code once per threshold and stacks the results into one data frame. Your version will need p_hat instead of pred, and recid instead of two_year_recid.

Code 
rates_at <- function(data, cutoff) {
  data %>%
    mutate(pred_50 = as.integer(p_hat >= cutoff)) %>%
    summarize(
      threshold   = cutoff,
      sensitivity = sum(pred_50 == 1 & recid == 1) / sum(recid == 1),
      specificity = sum(pred_50 == 0 & recid == 0) / sum(recid == 0),
      accuracy    = mean(pred_50 == recid)
    )
}

thresholds <- seq(0.30, 0.80, by = 0.05)
sweep <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(t) rates_at(test, t))
sweep

4.4 Plot the ROC curve for my_fit on the test set with pROC and report the AUC. In one sentence: what does the AUC tell you, and what doesn’t it tell you about the decision the department has to make?

Code 
library(pROC)

roc_obj <- roc(test$recid, test$p_hat, quiet = TRUE)
auc(roc_obj)
Area under the curve: 0.7037
Code 
ggroc(roc_obj, legacy.axes = TRUE) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "False positive rate (1 = specificity)",
       y = "True positive rate (sensitivity)",
       title = "Rearrest prediction on the test set") +
  theme_minimal()

Your answer: An AUC of 0.704 means the model ranks a randomly chosen rearrested person above a randomly chosen person who was not rearrested about 70% of the time, counting ties as half, but it does not tell the department which threshold to use.

Part 5: Is it race-blind?

Race isn’t in your model. Now check the errors by race on the test set.

5.1 At the threshold of 0.5, compute for each race: the share labeled high risk, the share actually rearrested, the false positive rate (labeled high risk, not rearrested, out of everyone not rearrested), and the false negative rate.

Code 
race_rates <- function(data, threshold){
  data %>%
    mutate(flag = as.integer(p_hat >= threshold)) %>%
    group_by(Race) %>%
    summarize(
      threshold = threshold,
      n = n(),
      high_risk = mean(flag),
      base_rate = mean(recid),
      fpr = sum(flag == 1 & recid == 0) / sum(recid == 0),
      fnr = sum(flag == 0 & recid == 1) / sum(recid == 1),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

race_rates(test, 0.50)
# A tibble: 2 × 7
  Race  threshold     n high_risk base_rate   fpr   fnr
  <chr>     <dbl> <int>     <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 BLACK       0.5  4534     0.726     0.582 0.585 0.173
2 WHITE       0.5  3273     0.674     0.564 0.498 0.190

Part 6: Does it hold up in places it hasn’t seen?

Use leave-one-PUMA-group-out cross-validation on the training set, the same recipe as Week 10’s leave-one-district-out.

Code 
pumas <- levels(train$puma)

cv_puma <- map_dfr(pumas, function(u) {
  cv_train <- train %>% filter(puma != u)
  cv_test  <- train %>% filter(puma == u)

  fit <- glm(formula(my_fit), family = binomial, data = cv_train)

  cv_test %>%
    mutate(pred = as.integer(predict(fit, newdata = cv_test,
                                     type = "response") >= 0.5)) %>%
    summarize(puma       = u,
              n          = n(),
              share_black = mean(Race == "BLACK"),
              accuracy   = mean(pred == recid),
              fpr        = sum(pred == 1 & recid == 0) / sum(recid == 0))
})

6.1 Plot each PUMA group’s false positive rate against its share of Black parolees. What pattern, if any, do you see?

Code 
cor(cv_puma$share_black, cv_puma$fpr)
[1] 0.3995608
Code 
ggplot(cv_puma, aes(share_black, fpr)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Share of Black parolees",
       y = "False positive rate at 0.50") +
  theme_minimal()

Your answer: Across 25 held-out PUMA groups, false positive rates ranged from 42.3% to 60.5%. Groups with a higher share of Black parolees tended to have higher false positive rates, with a correlation of 0.40 and considerable variation.

6.2 If you put puma itself into the model as a predictor, would that make the model more or less race-blind? Make an argument using what you found in 6.1. (You may test it, but you don’t have to.)

Your answer: Adding puma could make the model less race-blind in practice. The share of Black parolees ranged from 13.9% to 87.2% across areas, so location could carry information associated with race. The plot shows an existing association with false positive rates. A separate test would be needed to see how adding puma changes the racial error gap.

Part 7: The memo

Write a memo (400–600 words) to the Department of Community Supervision. It must:

  1. Pick a threshold for Use A and a threshold for Use B, and defend each using the cost of a false positive and a false negative in that use. Cite your own numbers from Parts 4 and 5.
  2. Tell them whether “the model doesn’t use race” means it treats Black and white parolees the same, using your Part 5 results.
  3. End with one sentence: “I would / would not deploy this for Use , unless .”

Write to a deputy commissioner, not to a statistician. No code, no jargon you haven’t explained.

Your memo: I recommend evaluating a 0.70 threshold for more restrictive supervision and piloting a 0.40 threshold for voluntary reentry outreach. The model estimates each person’s chance of rearrest within three years. In the test group, 57.4% of people were rearrested. The threshold should reflect what the department does when someone is flagged.

For Use A, a false positive could mean that someone who is never rearrested still has to take unpaid time off to report more often or wear an electronic monitor. Raising the threshold from 0.50 to 0.70 reduced the number of people who were flagged but never rearrested from 1,820 to 559. At 0.70, however, the model flagged only 39.3% of people who were later rearrested. Missing those people means losing a chance to consider whether more supervision would help. I favor the higher threshold for evaluation because the restrictions carry an immediate cost, and the historical records cannot tell us how many rearrests those restrictions would prevent.

For Use B, I would use the lower threshold to offer a voluntary needs assessment. At 0.40, the model flagged 91.5% of people who were later rearrested, up from 82.0% at 0.50. A missed flag could mean that someone who needs housing or job placement never gets a call. Calling someone who is never rearrested takes staff time, though that person may still need help. Because the threshold flags 82.0% of the test group, I would use the call to identify needs and assign scarce appointments based on those needs. People below the threshold should still be able to request assistance.

Omitting race did not produce equal error rates. At 0.50, among people who were never rearrested, 58.5% of Black parolees and 49.8% of white parolees were flagged. At the proposed supervision threshold of 0.70, the rates fell to 18.1% and 15.1%, respectively. At the proposed service threshold of 0.40, the model missed 7.5% of Black parolees and 10.0% of white parolees who were later rearrested. In a service pilot, I would track who gets a call, who receives an appointment, and who actually gets help, with results reported by race. The pilot should also measure whether the services help people find stable housing or work, since the score predicts rearrest rather than those outcomes.

I would not deploy this for Use A, unless an independent evaluation showed that the public safety benefits justify the added restrictions and that racial disparities meet a standard the department sets in advance.

Supervision_Risk_Score_First is the score Georgia’s existing risk tool assigned at the start of supervision. Treat a score of 7 or higher as “high risk” and compute its false positive rates by race on the test set. Does the state’s current tool look better or worse than yours?

Code 
test %>%
  filter(!is.na(Supervision_Risk_Score_First)) %>%
  mutate(state_flag = as.integer(Supervision_Risk_Score_First >= 7)) %>%
  group_by(Race) %>%
  summarize(

# The scenario

The Georgia Department of Community Supervision is considering a risk model to guide parole decisions. Every person released to parole would get a predicted probability of being **rearrested within three years**. The department has two proposed uses:

- **Use A:** people above a threshold get **more restrictive supervision** (more check-ins, electronic monitoring, faster revocation).
- **Use B:** people above a threshold get **priority for reentry services** (housing assistance, job placement, a case manager).

The department has promised that the model **will not use race**. You've been hired to build it and to tell them whether that promise means what they think it means.

**What you're turning in:** this rendered document, published in the `assignments/` folder of your portfolio.

**How this assignment works:** it has less scaffolding than earlier ones. The **Week 11 lab** (COMPAS) is your fully worked example: almost every step here has a matching step there. Where the NIJ data behaves differently from COMPAS, the instructions below tell you. Everywhere else, adapt the lab code yourself.

| A5 part | Week 11 lab step |
|---|---|
| 3.1 odds ratios | Step 3 |
| 4.1 predictions + confusion matrix | Steps 4–5 |
| 4.3 threshold sweep | Step 5 (`rates_at()`) |
| 4.4 ROC + AUC | Step 6 |
| 5.1–5.2 errors by race | Step 7 |
| 5.3 what carries race in | Step 8 |

Two differences from the lab: the outcome is called **`recid`** (not `two_year_recid`), and you **fit on `train` and evaluate on `test`**. In the lab we fit and scored on the same data. So every `predict()` in Parts 4 and 5 needs `newdata = test`.


# The data

The National Institute of Justice's **Recidivism Forecasting Challenge** data: 25,835 people released from Georgia prisons to parole supervision, 2013–2015. Download the CSV from Canvas, put it in your portfolio's `data/` folder, and rename it `nij_recidivism.csv`.

A few things to know before you start:

- **Race is recorded only as Black or white.** The data includes no one else.
- **Counts are top-coded:** "10 or more" prior felony arrests is stored as text. `parse_number()` turns it into 10, which undercounts people with many more.
- **`Residence_PUMA`** is not a census PUMA code. NIJ grouped Georgia's PUMAs into 25 areas and numbered them 1–25 to protect privacy. You can use it to group people by place, but you can't map it.
- **`Training_Sample`** is NIJ's own train/test split. Use it.

# Part 1: Load and clean


```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)

# rendering inside the project runs from the portfolio root; standalone runs
# from this folder, so check both
data_csv <- if (file.exists("assignment6-data/nij_recidivism.csv")) {
  "assignment6-data/nij_recidivism.csv"
} else {
  "assignments/assignment6-data/nij_recidivism.csv"
}

nij <- read_csv(data_csv) %>%
  mutate(
    recid              = as.integer(Recidivism_Within_3years),
    male               = as.integer(Gender == "M"),
    age_group          = factor(Age_at_Release),
    prison_years       = factor(Prison_Years,
                                levels = c("Less than 1 year", "1-2 years",
                                           "Greater than 2 to 3 years",
                                           "More than 3 years")),
    prior_fel_arrests  = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Felony),
    prior_misd_arrests = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Misd),
    puma               = factor(Residence_PUMA)
  )

train <- nij %>% filter(Training_Sample == 1)
test  <- nij %>% filter(Training_Sample == 0)
```

**1.1** How many people are in `train` and in `test`? What share of each was rearrested within three years?

```{r}
nij %>%
  mutate(sample = if_else(Training_Sample == 1, "train", "test")) %>%
  group_by(sample) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), rearrested = sum(recid),
            share_rearrested = mean(recid), .groups = "drop")
```

*Your answer:* The training set has 18,028 people, 57.80% were rearrested within three years. The test set has 7,807 people, 57.42% were rearrested.

**1.2** Look at `Gang_Affiliated`. How many values are missing, and who are they? (Hint: cross-tabulate it with `Gender`.) What would happen to your sample if you added this variable to a model without handling the missing values?

```{r}
with(nij, table(Gender, missing_gang = is.na(Gang_Affiliated)))
```

*Your answer:* All 3,167 missing values are for women. Adding Gang_Affiliated as is would exclude all 2,217 women from the training fit and leave all 950 women in the test set without predictions.

# Part 2: What would you know at the moment of decision?

The parole decision happens **at release**. Some columns in this file were recorded **during** the three years of supervision that followed.

**2.1** Sort every predictor column into one of two lists. You don't need code; use `names(nij)` and the column names.

| Known at release | Recorded during supervision (leakage) |
|---|---|
| `Gender`, `Race`, `Age_at_Release`, `Residence_PUMA`, `Gang_Affiliated` | `Violations_ElectronicMonitoring`, `Violations_Instruction`, `Violations_FailToReport`, `Violations_MoveWithoutPermission`, `Delinquency_Reports` |
| `Supervision_Risk_Score_First`, `Supervision_Level_First`, `Education_Level`, `Dependents`, `Prison_Offense`, `Prison_Years` | `Program_Attendances`, `Program_UnexcusedAbsences`, `Residence_Changes` |
| All eight `Prior_Arrest_Episodes_*` and all eight `Prior_Conviction_Episodes_*` columns | `Avg_Days_per_DrugTest`, `DrugTests_THC_Positive`, `DrugTests_Cocaine_Positive`, `DrugTests_Meth_Positive`, `DrugTests_Other_Positive` |
| `Prior_Revocations_Parole`, `Prior_Revocations_Probation`, `Condition_MH_SA`, `Condition_Cog_Ed`, `Condition_Other` | `Percent_Days_Employed`, `Jobs_Per_Year`, `Employment_Exempt` |

**2.2** Pick one variable from the right-hand column and explain, in two sentences, why including it would make your model look better than it really is. 

*Your answer:* `Percent_Days_Employed` is measured after release, and rearrest can cut the observation period short. Including it would give the model future information and make its test performance look better than it would be at release.

# Part 3: Build a race-blind model

Start from this model.

```{r}
#| label: base-model
base_fit <- glm(recid ~ male + age_group + prison_years +
                  prior_fel_arrests + prior_misd_arrests,
                family = binomial,
                data = train)

summary(base_fit)
```

**3.1** Exponentiate the coefficients. Interpret the odds ratio for `prior_fel_arrests` in one sentence, using the word *odds* correctly.

```{r}
exp(coef(base_fit))
```

*Your answer:* Holding the other predictors fixed, each additional recorded prior felony arrest multiplies the estimated odds of rearrest by 1.182, an 18.2% increase in the odds.

**3.2** Constant on the odds, not on the probability. Use `predict(..., type = "response")` with `newdata` to compute the predicted probability for two made-up people, then add one prior felony arrest to each:

- a man, age 23–27, 1–2 years in prison, 2 prior felony arrests, 1 misdemeanor arrest
- a man, age 48 or older, 1–2 years in prison, 2 prior felony arrests, 1 misdemeanor arrest

How much does one more arrest change each person's probability? Why are the two changes different?

```{r}
people <- tibble(
  male               = c(1, 1),
  age_group          = factor(c("23-27", "48 or older"), levels = levels(nij$age_group)),
  prison_years       = factor(c("1-2 years", "1-2 years"), levels = levels(nij$prison_years)),
  prior_fel_arrests  = c(2, 2),
  prior_misd_arrests = c(1, 1)
)

people_plus_one <- people %>%
  mutate(prior_fel_arrests = prior_fel_arrests +1)

people %>%
  transmute(
    age_group,
    before = predict(base_fit, newdata = people, type = "response"),
    after = predict(base_fit, newdata = people_plus_one, type = "response"),
    change_pp = 100 * (after - before)
  )
```

*Your answer:* The 23–27-year-old goes from 56.45% to 60.51%, up 4.06 percentage points. The person aged 48 or older goes from 17.86% to 20.45%, up 2.59 points. The same odds multiplier produces a larger probability change near 50%.

**3.3** Improve the model. Add at least **three** predictors from your "known at release" list. Keep race out. Call it `my_fit`. In two or three sentences, say what you added and why you expected each one to help.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Check for missing values before you add a variable
Some columns have blanks: `Prison_Offense` is missing for about 1 in 8 people, and `Supervision_Level_First` for about 1 in 15. If you add one as it is, `glm()` **silently drops** those people from training, and `predict()` returns `NA` for them in `test`. Then `mean()` gives `NA` in Parts 4–6, and `table()` quietly leaves them out. Either leave the variable out, or keep the blanks as their own category, for example `mutate(offense = replace_na(Prison_Offense, "Missing"))`. Whichever you choose, say so in your answer.
:::

```{r}
#| label: my-model
add_predictors <- function(data){
  data %>%
    mutate(
      education = factor(Education_Level),
      prior_violent_arrests = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Violent),
      prior_property_arrests = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Property)
    )
}
train <- add_predictors(train)
test <- add_predictors(test)

added <- c("education", "prior_violent_arrests", "prior_property_arrests")
stopifnot(!anyNA(train[added]), !anyNA(test[added]))

my_fit <- glm(recid ~ male + age_group + prison_years + prior_fel_arrests + 
    prior_misd_arrests + education + prior_violent_arrests + prior_property_arrests,
  family = binomial, 
  data = train, 
  na.action = na.fail
)

summary(my_fit)
```

*Your answer:* I added education because it may reflect access to employment, and prior violent and property arrests because each describes a different kind of arrest history. These predictors were complete in both splits. I left out race and the incomplete gang affiliation, prison offense, and initial supervision level fields.

# Part 4: Choosing a threshold

**4.1** Add a column `p_hat` to `test` with predicted probabilities from `my_fit`, and a column `pred_50` that flags anyone at or above 0.5. (Parts 5 and 6 use these column names.) Then make a confusion matrix and compute sensitivity and specificity.

```{r}
test <- test %>%
  mutate(
    p_hat = predict(my_fit, newdata = test, type = "response"),
    pred_50 = as.integer(p_hat >= 0.5)
  )

table(predicted = test$pred_50, actual = test$recid)

test %>%
  summarize(
    sensitivity = sum(pred_50 == 1 & recid == 1) / sum(recid == 1),
    specificity = sum(pred_50 == 0 & recid == 0) / sum(recid == 0),
    accuracy    = mean(pred_50 == recid)
  )

```

*Your answer:* Sensitivity was 82.0% and specificity was 45.2%.

**4.2** What share of the test set does your model label "high risk" at 0.5? Compare it to the share actually rearrested. What does that tell you about 0.5 as a default for this data?

*Your answer:* The 0.50 cutoff flagged 70.4% of the test set, while 57.4% were rearrested. It also flagged 54.8% of people who were not rearrested, making it a poor automatic default for restrictive supervision.

**4.3** Compute sensitivity and specificity for every threshold from 0.30 to 0.80 in steps of 0.05, and plot both lines on one chart with threshold on the x-axis.

Hint: in the lab you called `rates_at()` three times by hand. Here you need eleven thresholds. `map_dfr(thresholds, function(t) ...)` runs the same code once per threshold and stacks the results into one data frame. Your version will need `p_hat` instead of `pred`, and `recid` instead of `two_year_recid`.

```{r}
rates_at <- function(data, cutoff) {
  data %>%
    mutate(pred_50 = as.integer(p_hat >= cutoff)) %>%
    summarize(
      threshold   = cutoff,
      sensitivity = sum(pred_50 == 1 & recid == 1) / sum(recid == 1),
      specificity = sum(pred_50 == 0 & recid == 0) / sum(recid == 0),
      accuracy    = mean(pred_50 == recid)
    )
}

thresholds <- seq(0.30, 0.80, by = 0.05)
sweep <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(t) rates_at(test, t))
sweep

sweep%>%
  pivot_longer(c(sensitivity, specificity),
               names_to = "metric", values_to = "rate") %>%
  ggplot(aes(threshold, rate, color = metric)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = thresholds) +
  labs(x = "Threshold", y = "Rate", color = NULL) + 
  theme_minimal()

```

**4.4** Plot the ROC curve for `my_fit` on the test set with `pROC` and report the AUC. In one sentence: what does the AUC tell you, and what doesn't it tell you about the decision the department has to make?

```{r}
library(pROC)

roc_obj <- roc(test$recid, test$p_hat, quiet = TRUE)
auc(roc_obj)

ggroc(roc_obj, legacy.axes = TRUE) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "False positive rate (1 = specificity)",
       y = "True positive rate (sensitivity)",
       title = "Rearrest prediction on the test set") +
  theme_minimal()

```

*Your answer:* An AUC of 0.704 means the model ranks a randomly chosen rearrested person above a randomly chosen person who was not rearrested about 70% of the time, counting ties as half, but it does not tell the department which threshold to use.

# Part 5: Is it race-blind?

Race isn't in your model. Now check the errors by race on the **test set**.

**5.1** At the threshold of 0.5, compute for each race: the share labeled high risk, the share actually rearrested, the **false positive rate** (labeled high risk, not rearrested, out of everyone not rearrested), and the **false negative rate**.

```{r}
race_rates <- function(data, threshold){
  data %>%
    mutate(flag = as.integer(p_hat >= threshold)) %>%
    group_by(Race) %>%
    summarize(
      threshold = threshold,
      n = n(),
      high_risk = mean(flag),
      base_rate = mean(recid),
      fpr = sum(flag == 1 & recid == 0) / sum(recid == 0),
      fnr = sum(flag == 0 & recid == 1) / sum(recid == 1),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

race_rates(test, 0.50)
```

**5.2** Repeat 5.1 at two other thresholds from your sweep. Does the gap between groups close, stay, or flip?

```{r}
bind_rows(
  race_rates(test, 0.40),
  race_rates(test, 0.70)
)
```

*Your answer:* The false positive rate remained higher for Black parolees, but the gap narrowed from 10.1 to 2.9 percentage points using unrounded rates. The false negative rate went from lower for Black parolees at 0.40 to slightly higher at 0.70.

**5.3** Investigate at least two candidates by comparing their distributions by race. Possibilities include age, prior arrests, prison offense, and place (`puma`). Show your evidence with a table or chart for each.

```{r}
test %>%
  group_by(Race) %>%
  count(age_group) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  print(n = Inf)
test %>%
  group_by(Race) %>%
  count(prior_fel_arrests) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  print(n = Inf)
```

*Your answer:* In the test set, 32.6% of Black parolees and 21.3% of white parolees were under 28. The shares with 10 or more prior felony arrests were 24.0% and 22.8%, respectively. Both inputs vary by race, and the model gives higher scores to younger people and people with more prior felony arrests, holding other inputs fixed.


# Part 6: Does it hold up in places it hasn't seen?

Use leave-one-PUMA-group-out cross-validation **on the training set**, the same recipe as Week 10's leave-one-district-out.

```{r}
pumas <- levels(train$puma)

cv_puma <- map_dfr(pumas, function(u) {
  cv_train <- train %>% filter(puma != u)
  cv_test  <- train %>% filter(puma == u)

  fit <- glm(formula(my_fit), family = binomial, data = cv_train)

  cv_test %>%
    mutate(pred = as.integer(predict(fit, newdata = cv_test,
                                     type = "response") >= 0.5)) %>%
    summarize(puma       = u,
              n          = n(),
              share_black = mean(Race == "BLACK"),
              accuracy   = mean(pred == recid),
              fpr        = sum(pred == 1 & recid == 0) / sum(recid == 0))
})
```

**6.1** Plot each PUMA group's false positive rate against its share of Black parolees. What pattern, if any, do you see?

```{r}
cor(cv_puma$share_black, cv_puma$fpr)

ggplot(cv_puma, aes(share_black, fpr)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Share of Black parolees",
       y = "False positive rate at 0.50") +
  theme_minimal()
```

*Your answer:* Across 25 held-out PUMA groups, false positive rates ranged from 42.3% to 60.5%. Groups with a higher share of Black parolees tended to have higher false positive rates, with a correlation of 0.40 and considerable variation.

**6.2** If you put `puma` itself into the model as a predictor, would that make the model more or less race-blind? Make an argument using what you found in 6.1. (You may test it, but you don't have to.)

*Your answer:* Adding `puma` could make the model less race-blind in practice. The share of Black parolees ranged from 13.9% to 87.2% across areas, so location could carry information associated with race. The plot shows an existing association with false positive rates. A separate test would be needed to see how adding `puma` changes the racial error gap.
